prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "MICROSOFT CORP" (ticker MSFT). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Microsoft has several Rule Breaker traits (top dog in enterprise software and a leader in cloud and AI, strong management, a lasting advantage), but it is a 50-year-old Rule Maker rather than a disruptor of an emerging industry. Its recent price momentum is weak: the stock rose 6.4% over 52 weeks versus 17.3% for the S&P 500.
summaries.buffett: Microsoft fits Buffett's tenets well: a durable franchise with high switching costs, consistent results, ROIC of about 26%, rational capital allocation under Satya Nadella and a dividend raised every year. The cautions are heavy AI capex, which has cut free cash flow to $67.0B against $133.7B of net income in FY2026, and a price of about 30 times earnings that offers no clear margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would appreciate Microsoft's entrenched position in workplace software and cloud and its culture turnaround under Nadella. Inverting shows few ways it could fail outright, but real risks in its dependence on OpenAI and in whether more than $100B a year of AI capex earns adequate returns.
summaries.lynch: Microsoft is a Lynch stalwart, arguably a fast-growing one, with a story anyone can follow (Office, Windows, Azure, Copilot). At a P/E of 30.3 and a PEG of about 1.75 it is not cheap by his measure, and it is heavily followed rather than overlooked.
summaries.fisher: Microsoft fits Fisher's 15 points strongly: it keeps launching new growth products (Azure, Teams, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365 Copilot), has an outstanding enterprise sales organisation, operating margins near 47% and a long-term-minded CEO. Fisher would check whether its large R&D and AI spending keeps paying off as Azure competes with AWS and Google Cloud.
summaries.graham: Microsoft passes Graham's tests for size, ten years of profits, a dividend record of more than 20 years (since 2003) and strong EPS growth. It fails on price: a P/E of 30.3 and P/B of 9.1 multiply to about 276, far above his 22.5 limit.
summaries.thiel: Microsoft has strong distribution, a durable near-monopoly in office software and PC operating systems, and an AI edge through OpenAI. It is not clearly ten times better than rivals in cloud or AI, and its opportunities are well known rather than a unique secret.
summaries.gerstner: Microsoft is a core beneficiary of the AI and cloud platform shift Gerstner emphasises, with Azure passing $100B of annual revenue and commercial backlog of $678B. On his growth-adjusted valuation lens it is reasonably priced at a forward P/E of about 27.5 for revenue growth near 18%, though the AI capex burden is a concern he has raised about the sector.
summaries.druckenmiller: Microsoft's fundamentals are improving (FY2026 revenue +17.8%, Azure +43% in the June quarter), but the stock has lagged the market over the past year, which runs against Druckenmiller's preference for price confirmation. He would weigh Azure acceleration against concerns about capex and OpenAI.
summaries.smith: Microsoft is a textbook Fundsmith-style holding: high returns on capital, high margins, low leverage, recurring revenue and decades of resilience. Its free-cash-flow yield has fallen to about 1.7% as capex rose, which makes the 'don't overpay' test harder to pass.
summaries.greenblatt: Microsoft has a good return on capital (ROIC about 26%), but its earnings yield is low: EV/EBIT of 26.3 implies about 3.8%. It would rank only moderately on the Magic Formula.
summaries.akre: Microsoft fits all three legs of Akre's stool: an extraordinary business, a talented and shareholder-minded CEO, and large reinvestment opportunities in cloud and AI. The question is whether today's very heavy AI reinvestment will earn returns as high as its past ones.
summaries.pabrai: Microsoft is a high-quality, widely owned company priced at 30 times earnings, not the cheap, distressed, low-risk bet that Pabrai's Dhandho framework seeks. Its recent underperformance is not a deep, temporary setback of the kind he looks for.
summaries.wood: Microsoft is a leading AI platform through Azure, Copilot and its OpenAI stake, and it is also working on quantum computing (Majorana 1). ARK tends to see it as an incumbent rather than a pure disruptive innovator, and it has little exposure to robotics, energy storage, blockchain or sequencing.
summaries.ackman: Microsoft fits much of Ackman's checklist: simple to understand, predictable, recurring revenue, high barriers to entry and low leverage. Its heavy AI capex and reliance on OpenAI reduce the free-cash-flow predictability he values.
summaries.sleep: Microsoft spreads its software and data-centre costs over hundreds of millions of users, a scale advantage, and bundles more features into Microsoft 365. It mostly captures these gains as margin and price increases rather than passing them back, so it fits Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model only partly.
summaries.valentine: Microsoft serves huge markets with products that solve large problems for businesses, which matches Valentine's criteria. It is now a mature giant rather than the kind of young, market-creating company Sequoia backed.

momentum.evidence: MSFT closed at $543.45 on 13 October 2026, up 6.4% over 52 weeks, lagging the S&P 500's 17.3% price gain over the same period.

g4.evidence: Microsoft is led by Satya Nadella, widely seen as one of the best CEOs of his generation, and partners with OpenAI, NVIDIA and AMD.

g6.evidence: Most of the 56 covering analysts rate it Strong Buy with an average target of $589.60, above the price; it is not commonly called overvalued.

simple.evidence: Microsoft sells widely used software (Office, Windows), cloud services (Azure) and games, a business most generalists can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $168.1B in FY2021 to $331.8B in FY2026, with high profitability throughout.

integrity.evidence: Microsoft has a single share class, strong governance, a dividend raised every year and pay tied to performance, and Nadella is known for candour with shareholders.

b6.evidence: It mostly grows organically, but it has made very large acquisitions such as LinkedIn ($26B, 2016) and Activision Blizzard ($69B, 2023), the latter followed by gaming weakness.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 26% and ROE 34%, with debt/equity of only 0.29 (StockAnalysis, October 2026).

fcf.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was $67.0B, only about half of $133.7B net income, because capital spending on AI data centres has risen sharply.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings funded Azure, which passed $100B of annual revenue, and market value rose to about $4.0 trillion, far more than the earnings retained.

safety.evidence: At 30.3 times trailing earnings and a 1.7% free-cash-flow yield, the price is not well below a conservative estimate of value.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of 27.5 for consensus revenue growth of about 18% in FY2027 is reasonable for its quality, but not cheap.

mu5.evidence: Its diversified, recurring, enterprise-embedded revenue and strong balance sheet mean few ways to fail; the main risks are OpenAI dependence and AI capex returns.

reinvest.evidence: It is reinvesting heavily in AI data centres (about $116B of FY2026 capex) at a current ROIC of about 26%, but returns on this new spending are not yet proven.

ly2.evidence: Microsoft is a stalwart with fast-grower traits: a giant whose story is cloud and AI growth on top of entrenched Office and Windows franchises.

ly3.evidence: Its P/E of 30.3 is roughly in line with FY2026 EPS growth of 31.6% ($13.64 to $17.95), but that included about $5B of OpenAI-related gains and the PEG on forecasts is about 1.75.

runway.evidence: Azure grew 43% in the June 2026 quarter and commercial remaining performance obligation reached $678B, up 84%, giving years of growth visibility.

ly7.evidence: The diluted share count fell only 0.16% over the past year, and insiders own about 0.03% and generally sell rather than buy.

ly8.evidence: Microsoft is one of the most widely owned and followed stocks, covered by 56 analysts.

fi2.evidence: As Windows and Office matured it built Azure, Teams, Dynamics 365, GitHub Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot.

fi3.evidence: R&D produced Azure, now over $100B of annual revenue, and AI products such as GitHub Copilot, though its own AI models trail OpenAI, Google and Anthropic.

fi4.evidence: Its enterprise sales force and partner network are among the strongest in software, selling bundles of Microsoft 365, security and Azure to most large organisations.

longterm.evidence: Nadella moved to cloud in 2014 and invested in OpenAI from 2019, and is spending heavily on AI infrastructure despite the hit to free cash flow.

gr1.evidence: Microsoft had $331.8B of FY2026 revenue and a market capitalization of about $4.0 trillion.

ni10.evidence: Microsoft has been profitable in every one of the last ten fiscal years, with EPS ranging from $2.13 (FY2018, tax-reform charge) to $17.95 (FY2026).

gr4.evidence: Microsoft has paid a dividend every year since 2003, more than 20 years, and paid $3.64 per share in FY2026.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $2.56 in FY2016 to $17.95 in FY2026, about sevenfold.

gr6.evidence: The trailing P/E is 30.3, about double Graham's limit of about 15.

gr7.evidence: P/E of 30.3 times P/B of 9.1 is about 276, far above Graham's 22.5 ceiling.

th1.evidence: Azure, Copilot and Teams compete closely with AWS, Google and ChatGPT and are not ten times better than the next best.

timing.evidence: Its early OpenAI partnership and Azure scale positioned it well for generative AI, with Azure growing 43% in the June 2026 quarter.

th3.evidence: Microsoft started by dominating the small early market for PC operating systems (MS-DOS) and expanded into Windows, Office, servers and cloud.

team.evidence: Satya Nadella, CEO since 2014, is widely regarded as world-class, having led the turnaround to cloud and AI with CFO Amy Hood.

th5.evidence: Its global enterprise sales force, reseller partners and default position in Windows give it unmatched reach to business customers.

durable.evidence: Windows and Office have stayed the workplace standard for over 30 years and enterprise switching costs are high, though AI-native tools are a long-term risk.

th7.evidence: Its 2019 bet on OpenAI was an early insight others missed, but its main opportunities in cloud and AI are now widely seen.

trend.evidence: Microsoft is one of the leading beneficiaries of cloud and AI, with Azure passing $100B of annual revenue in FY2026.

dr1.evidence: Revenue growth sped up from 14.9% in FY2025 to 17.8% in FY2026, but forward EPS is only about 10% above trailing EPS, which included OpenAI-related gains.

dr2.evidence: A $678B commercial backlog and Copilot adoption could make it look better in two years, but much of this is visible to investors already.

dr4.evidence: Microsoft's net cash position makes it little affected by rates, but enterprise IT budgets depend on the economy.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include Q1 FY2027 results in late October 2026, Azure capacity coming online and growth in paid Copilot seats.

dr7.evidence: Its quality supports a large position, but the stock's lag over the past year and AI capex uncertainty temper conviction.

gm.evidence: Trailing gross margin is 67.9%, high and a sign of pricing power, though it has slipped as AI infrastructure costs rise.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 1.7% ($67.0B on a $4.0 trillion market cap), low because capex is elevated; on operating cash flow of $182.9B it is about 4.5%.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is 26.3, an earnings yield of about 3.8%, which is low by Magic Formula standards.

pa2.evidence: The stock has lagged as free cash flow fell from $74.1B (FY2024) to $67.0B (FY2026) amid heavy AI capex, which may prove temporary if that spending earns good returns.

pa4.evidence: With recurring enterprise revenue, debt/equity of 0.29 and decades of resilience, the chance of permanent loss at the business level is small.

wo1.evidence: Microsoft is a leader in AI through Azure AI, Microsoft 365 Copilot, GitHub Copilot and its stake in OpenAI.

wo2.evidence: The cost of AI inference on Azure falls as volumes grow, but Microsoft's own product prices are rising rather than falling.

wo3.evidence: It combines cloud, AI and quantum computing research, but has little presence in robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomics.

wo4.evidence: AI agents and Copilot could expand its addressable market substantially, but many-times growth within five years is uncertain for a company of its size.

ac3.evidence: Its software and cloud revenue is largely recurring and insulated from commodity prices and interest rates, though energy and chip costs affect data centres.

ns1.evidence: Microsoft bundles more features into Microsoft 365 at scale, but it also raises prices, keeping much of its scale benefit.

ns4.evidence: Its enterprise position should stay strong, but it is unclear that it will be clearly stronger in 10-20 years given AI-native competition and OpenAI independence.

va2.evidence: It solves the large problem of running secure, reliable IT, productivity software and cloud infrastructure for most of the world's organisations.
